title: SmolVLA: A vision-language-action model for affordable and efficient robotics
params_and_backbone: 0.45B total (Table 5; also 0.24B and 2.25B variants). VLM = SmolVLM-2 (SigLIP vision encoder + SmolLM2 decoder); only first N=L/2 VLM layers used (last L-N skipped); 64 visual tokens per frame (global image, no tiling). Action expert hidden size 0.75×d of VLM (expert param count UNVERIFIED).
action_generation: flow matching (conditional flow-matching transformer, interleaved cross- and causal self-attention); 10 flow steps at inference; chunk size n=50 by default (ablation: n=10 gave higher LIBERO avg 84.0 vs 80.3 for n=50)
efficiency_lever: Model size (small VLM, layer skipping to L/2, 64 visual tokens/frame, smaller expert) + asynchronous inference that decouples chunk prediction from execution (RobotClient/PolicyServer, queue threshold g triggers new chunk requests early); trained only on ~23k community episodes (481 datasets, 22.9K episodes, 10.6M frames).
reported_gain: Async vs sync on SO-100: avg completion time 13.75 s -> 9.70 s (~30% faster), 19 vs 9 cubes in fixed-time episode, success 73.3% vs 78.3%. Vs pi0: 'around 40% faster to train and consumes 6× less memory'. Runs on consumer-grade hardware (GPUs or even CPUs). Total project compute ~30k GPU hours; pretraining 200k steps, batch 256, 4 GPUs.
benchmark_success: LIBERO (S/O/G/L/avg): 0.45B 90/96/92/71/87.3 (no robotics pretraining); 2.25B avg 88.75; 0.24B avg 82.75. Baselines in same table: pi0 3.3B (robot-pretrained) 86.0, OpenVLA 7B 76.5, Octo 0.09B 75.1, Diffusion Policy 72.4. Meta-World avg: 0.45B 57.3 (pi0 3.5B 47.9-50.5, TinyVLA 31.6). Real SO-100 avg 78.3% (pi0 61.7%).
assumptions: Chunked execution is acceptable; async inference assumes a remote PolicyServer and that observations arriving mid-execution can be used to recompute the remaining chunk; pretraining data from a single low-cost robot type (SO100) community datasets.
tradeoffs: Async reduces wall-clock completion time but success dropped 78.3% -> 73.3% in the SO-100 async study; sim results without robotics pretraining; LIBERO-Long (71) remains the weakest suite for 0.45B.
open_questions: Authors: pretraining from a single robot type (SO100); ~23k trajectories much smaller than typical VLA datasets. (reviewer inference) How async chunk switching interacts with chunk discontinuities / stale actions (later addressed by A2C2, RTC); per-step latency on embedded CPU not reported in the parts read.

title: π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control
venue: arXiv (RSS 2025 per external listings; not stated on arXiv page read — UNVERIFIED)
params_and_backbone: 3.3B total: PaliGemma 3B VLM + ~300M action expert (width=1024, mlp dim=4096, initialized from scratch)
action_generation: flow matching; 10 forward Euler integration steps (δ=0.1) from noise at τ=0; action chunk H=50; up to 50 Hz control
efficiency_lever: Not an efficiency paper; uses a separate smaller action expert and chunked continuous actions (KV of observation prefix reused across 10 flow steps) to reach high-frequency control. Re-plans every 16 actions (20 Hz robots, every 0.8 s) or 25 actions (50 Hz robots, every 0.5 s).
reported_gain: Inference on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 (Appendix D, Table I): image encoders 14 ms, observation forward pass 32 ms, 10× action forward pass (flow) 27 ms, total on-board 73 ms; off-board +13 ms network = 86 ms.
benchmark_success: No LIBERO in original paper (headline results are bar charts on real tasks: shirt folding, bussing, box building, etc.; full pre-trained pi0 'more than 50% of the maximum score across all' complex multi-stage tasks). Third-party: SmolVLA paper reports pi0 3.3B LIBERO avg 86.0.
assumptions: Large pretraining mixture (>10,000 h; 903M timesteps own data, 7 robot configurations, 68 tasks; OXE/Bridge/DROID 9.1%); timestep sampling Beta((s−τ)/s;1.5,1) with s=0.999 emphasizes noisy timesteps; chunk executed open-loop between inference calls.
tradeoffs: 3.3B params and 73 ms/chunk on an RTX 4090 — needs a desktop GPU or off-board inference; open-loop execution of 16–25 actions between re-plans.
open_questions: Authors: not all tasks work reliably; unclear how much and what kind of data is needed. (reviewer inference) Latency vs. reactivity when execution horizon shrinks; whether 10 Euler steps can be reduced further without loss.

title: OpenVLA: An Open-Source Vision-Language-Action Model
first_author: Moo Jin Kim (co-first with Karl Pertsch, Siddharth Karamcheti)
venue: arXiv (CoRL 2024 per external listings; not stated in PDF read — UNVERIFIED)
params_and_backbone: 7B; Prismatic-7B VLM: fused DINOv2+SigLIP vision encoder (~600M, features concatenated channel-wise), 2-layer MLP projector, Llama 2 7B
action_generation: autoregressive tokens: each action dimension discretized into 256 bins (1st–99th quantile), mapped onto the 256 least-used Llama tokens; one action per step (7 tokens), no chunking
efficiency_lever: Parameter-efficient adaptation (LoRA, 1.4% of params) and memory-efficient inference via int8/int4 quantization; baseline efficiency reference for later work
reported_gain: vs RT-2-X (55B): +16.5% absolute task success across 29 tasks with 7× fewer params. LoRA: 1.4% params, matches full FT; 10–15 h on 1 A100 vs full FT 8 A100 × 5–15 h (8× compute reduction). Quantization (Table 2, BridgeData V2): bf16 71.3% / 16.8 GB; int8 58.1% / 10.2 GB; int4 71.9% / 7.0 GB; on A5000 int8 1.2 Hz, int4 3 Hz. ~6 Hz bf16 on RTX 4090 (no compilation/speculative decoding).
benchmark_success: 29-task real-robot eval vs RT-2-X (+16.5% abs). LIBERO fine-tuned (S/O/G/L/avg) 84.7/88.4/79.2/53.7/76.5 as reported in the SmolVLA paper's table (not verified in OpenVLA PDF excerpt read).
assumptions: Single-image observation, no proprioception or history; discretized actions sufficient; 970k OXE demonstrations for pretraining.
tradeoffs: Autoregressive per-dimension decoding limits throughput (~6 Hz on RTX 4090); int8 quantization hurt success (58.1%) and was slower (1.2 Hz) than int4 on A5000.
open_questions: Authors: need higher inference throughput for high-frequency control (e.g., ALOHA 50 Hz); single-image only; success typically <90%. (reviewer inference) Effect of action chunking/parallel decoding (later answered by OpenVLA-OFT).

title: Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success
venue: arXiv (RSS 2025 per external listings; not stated in PDF v2 read — UNVERIFIED)
params_and_backbone: OpenVLA 7B (Prismatic VLM: DINOv2+SigLIP + Llama 2 7B), fine-tuned with OFT recipe; OFT+ adds FiLM
action_generation: parallel decoding + regression: all chunk actions decoded in one forward pass (bidirectional, empty action embeddings), continuous actions via MLP head trained with L1 loss; chunk K=8 (LIBERO), K=25 (ALOHA); single forward pass
efficiency_lever: Replace autoregressive per-token decoding with parallel decoding + action chunking + continuous L1 regression (fine-tuning recipe, architecture unchanged backbone)
reported_gain: 26× action-generation throughput (abstract). Table II on NVIDIA A100, 7-D actions: OpenVLA 4.2 Hz / 0.2396 s -> +PD 15.9 Hz / 0.0629 s -> +PD&AC 108.8 Hz / 0.0735 s -> OFT (Cont-L1) 109.7 Hz / 0.0729 s -> +wrist img & proprio 71.4 Hz / 0.1120 s. ALOHA (A100): OFT+ 77.9 Hz, 0.321 s latency (vs OpenVLA 1.8 Hz, 0.543 s; pi0 291.6 Hz, 0.086 s).
benchmark_success: LIBERO S/O/G/L/avg: OpenVLA-OFT (wrist+state) 97.6/98.4/97.9/94.5/97.1 (vs OpenVLA FT 76.5; pi0 94.2; pi0-FAST 85.5; third-person only OFT 95.3). ALOHA (25 Hz): OFT+ outperforms pi0, RDT-1B, ACT, DP by up to 15% abs avg success.
assumptions: Unimodal-enough demonstrations so that L1 regression suffices; task-specific fine-tuning; A100-class GPU for reported throughput.
tradeoffs: Extra inputs (wrist image, proprio) cut throughput 109.7 -> 71.4 Hz; ALOHA latency (0.321 s) still higher than pi0 (0.086 s) despite higher success; FiLM needed for language grounding on ALOHA.
open_questions: Authors: L1 regression may struggle with truly multimodal action distributions; unclear whether OFT benefits extend to pretraining; unclear why language grounding fails on ALOHA but not LIBERO. (reviewer inference) Behaviour on edge GPUs not reported.

title: FAST: Efficient Action Tokenization for Vision-Language-Action Models
params_and_backbone: pi0-FAST: pi0 architecture on PaliGemma-3B (autoregressive 2B language backbone, no 300M flow expert); also applied to OpenVLA (Prismatic 7B)
action_generation: autoregressive tokens: per-dimension quantile normalization -> DCT -> scale & round (scale 10) -> low-frequency-first flattening -> BPE (vocab 1024); 1-second chunks (e.g., 15-step chunks on DROID at 15 Hz); ~30–60 tokens decoded per chunk
efficiency_lever: Compress action chunks into fewer, less-correlated tokens (DCT + BPE) to make autoregressive VLA training effective at high frequency; universal FAST+ tokenizer trained on ~1M 1-s action chunks
reported_gain: Tokens per 1-s chunk naive vs FAST (Table I): BridgeV2 35->20 (1.75×), DROID 105->29 (3.6×), Bussing 140->28 (5.0×), Shirt fold 700->53 (13.2×). pi0-FAST matches diffusion pi0 'while reducing training time by up to 5x' (5× fewer GPU hours); ~3× fewer training steps on table bussing. Inference on NVIDIA 4090: pi0-FAST ~750 ms per chunk vs ~100 ms for diffusion pi0.
benchmark_success: LIBERO: comparable to diffusion pi0 (numbers only in figures; not extracted). Third-party (OpenVLA-OFT Table): pi0+FAST fine-tuned LIBERO S/O/G/L/avg 96.4/96.8/88.6/60.2/85.5. DROID zero-shot generalist policy (exact SR not in text).
assumptions: Smooth, highly correlated action signals compressible in frequency domain; BPE trained per dataset unless FAST+ used.
tradeoffs: Training-efficiency gain comes at ~7.5× slower inference (~750 ms vs ~100 ms per chunk on 4090) due to autoregressive decoding of 30–60 tokens through the full backbone.
open_questions: Authors: combining compression with non-autoregressive decoding (e.g., diffusion) left to future work; only static manipulators tested on hardware; slower inference made evaluation significantly slower. (reviewer inference) Effect on dynamic tasks requiring <100 ms reaction.

title: TinyVLA: Towards Fast, Data-Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models for Robotic Manipulation
venue: IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (accepted Feb 2025, per PDF header)
params_and_backbone: TinyVLA-S/B/H: 422M/740M/1.3B total, 101M/138M/143M trainable (Table II); Pythia language backbone in a small VLM (70M–1.4B family); 3B PaliGemma variant only in ablation
action_generation: diffusion: Diffusion Policy head conditioned via 3-layer MLP on VLM features (denoising steps and chunk size not stated in text read — UNVERIFIED)
efficiency_lever: Small VLM backbone (<1.4B) + frozen VLM with LoRA on Q/K/V (5.0% of transformer params trainable) + diffusion head instead of autoregressive token decoding; no robot-data pretraining
reported_gain: Table IV, single A6000, per-action prediction: TinyVLA-1B 14 ms vs OpenVLA-7B 292 ms (~20×) and OpenVLA-1B 140 ms (~10×).
benchmark_success: Meta-World 50 tasks avg: TinyVLA-H 31.6% vs Diffusion Policy 10.5%. Real Franka 5 tasks: TinyVLA-H 94.0% vs OpenVLA 68.3% (+25.7). Bimanual UR5: OpenVLA 0%; TinyVLA-H ~47.8% by Table III (text says 44.5%) vs DP 38.2%.
assumptions: VLM pretrained only on vision-language data is sufficient when fine-tuned on task demos; per-task/multi-task fine-tuning data available.
tradeoffs: Smaller VLMs misinterpret instructions more often (0.4B variant); occasional failures under camera-view shift; OpenVLA slightly better on distant spatial generalization.
open_questions: (reviewer inference) Denoising-step count and chunk size not reported, so latency is not directly comparable across papers; internal inconsistencies in text vs tables (21.5 vs 21.1 pts; 44.5 vs 47.8%). No dedicated limitations section.

title: VLA-Cache: Efficient Vision-Language-Action Manipulation via Adaptive Token Caching
params_and_backbone: Applied to OpenVLA (7B), OpenVLA-OFT, CogACT (all Llama-2-based decoders)
action_generation: inherits base model (OpenVLA autoregressive tokens; OpenVLA-OFT parallel decoding+regression; CogACT diffusion head)
efficiency_lever: Reuse KV of visually static tokens across consecutive timesteps: cosine-similarity patch matching vs previous frame + top-k; exclude task-relevant tokens via text-to-vision attention; layer-adaptive reuse ratio from cumulative attention-entropy reduction
reported_gain: Abstract: 'up to 1.7× speedup in CUDA latency' and '15% increase in control frequency, with negligible loss on task success rate'. RTX 4090, BF16. LIBERO OpenVLA: FLOPs 1.864T->1.355T, latency 51.91->31.83 ms, 4.23->4.59 Hz. OpenVLA-OFT: 4.013T->3.097T, 79.05->62.59 ms, 65.10->78.98 Hz. SIMPLER CogACT (VM): 54.29->39.63 ms, 12.42->14.66 Hz. Real Kinova Jaco2 (OpenVLA): 64.16->51.85 ms.
benchmark_success: LIBERO avg: OpenVLA 75.0->74.7; OpenVLA-OFT 96.8->97.4. SIMPLER CogACT: VM 74.8->74.4, VA 61.3->62.3. Real robot avg 82.1->84.6.
assumptions: Consecutive frames share many static background patches; base decoder exposes per-layer attention/KV cache (Llama-2 style).
tradeoffs: Per-table gains are smaller than headline (OpenVLA latency 1.63×, control freq +8.5%; OFT 1.26×, +21%) — end-to-end Hz gain much smaller than CUDA-latency gain for OpenVLA; per-task drops possible (PickPot 95->90%).
open_questions: Authors: dynamic scenes (camera/background/object motion) increase non-reusable tokens and reduce gains; only three Llama-2-based VLAs tested. (reviewer inference) Interaction with action chunking (fewer inference calls) and with flow/diffusion experts.

title: DeeR-VLA: Dynamic Inference of Multimodal Large Language Models for Efficient Robot Execution
first_author: Yang Yue (equal contribution with Yulin Wang)
params_and_backbone: RoboFlamingo++ / OpenFlamingo, 3B (24 LLM layers) and 9B (32 layers) variants; multi-exit built on first 12 layers with 6 exit points; LSTM action head (window 12)
action_generation: other: regression via LSTM action head on intermediate MLLM features (one action per step)
efficiency_lever: Dynamic early exit: LLM layers split into groups with exits; stop at first exit whose predicted action is consistent with previous exit's; per-exit thresholds tuned from demonstrations or online Bayesian optimization under average-FLOPs / peak-FLOPs / GPU-memory budgets
reported_gain: Abstract: LLM computational cost reduced 5.2–6.5× and LLM GPU memory 2–6× 'without compromising performance'. LLM GFLOPs/action ~8.6–12.5 vs 31.2 baseline. On Nvidia V100: LLM inference 55 ms -> 17.5 ms (ABCD->D; 68.1% reduction), without early-exit code optimization. Activated-LLM memory ~2 GB for DeeR-S (3B).
benchmark_success: CALVIN avg successful length (DeeR / DeeR online / RoboFlamingo++): D->D 2.83/2.92/2.71; ABC->D 2.82/2.90/2.59; ABCD->D 4.13/4.13/4.07.
assumptions: Many timesteps are 'easy' and need fewer layers; adjacent-exit action consistency is a valid confidence proxy; threshold calibration data or online interaction available.
tradeoffs: Requires training the multi-exit model (perceiver sampler + cross-attention fine-tuned, backbone frozen) — not training-free; savings limited to the LLM (vision encoder cost unchanged); variable per-step latency.
open_questions: Authors: visual encoder cost also significant; experiments only on simulated benchmark (CALVIN). (reviewer inference) Worst-case latency guarantees for real-time control; applicability to chunked flow/diffusion VLAs.

title: EfficientVLA: Training-Free Acceleration and Compression for Vision-Language-Action Models
venue: arXiv (v1 'Preprint. Under review.'; later venue UNVERIFIED)
params_and_backbone: Applied to CogACT 7.63B (DINOv2+SigLIP vision, Llama2-7B language module, Diffusion Transformer action head); pruned to 4.86B (L=22) or 5.87B (L=28)
action_generation: diffusion (inherited CogACT DiT action head); action-head attention/MLP outputs cached and recomputed every 5 denoising steps
efficiency_lever: Training-free, three-part: (1) non-contiguous language-layer pruning by 1 − cos(input,output) importance + 25% MLP sparsity (PruneNet); (2) instruction-guided visual token selection (K_key=4 top-relevance + relevance/diversity fill; T=56 or 112 tokens kept); (3) temporal caching of diffusion-head intermediate features (interval 5)
reported_gain: Abstract: 1.93× inference speedup, FLOPs reduced to 28.9%, 0.6% success drop on SIMPLER. Table: L=22,T=56: 28.9% FLOPs, 1.93×, 4.86B params; L=28,T=112: 45.1% FLOPs, 1.59×, 5.87B. Inference time per step 0.2342 s -> 0.1213 s (Table 3). NVIDIA A40 GPUs.
benchmark_success: SIMPLER Visual Matching avg: CogACT 74.8% -> 74.2% (L=22,T=56) / 76.4% (L=28,T=112); Variant Aggregation 61.3% -> 61.2%.
assumptions: Redundancy exists in deep language layers, visual tokens and across denoising steps; access to attention maps for instruction-guided selection; diffusion head features change slowly between steps.
tradeoffs: Training-free so compression ceiling below training-aware methods; fixed cache interval trades acceleration vs action fidelity; per-task SR varies (e.g., Drawer Apple 53.8%).
open_questions: Authors: adaptive caching as future work; only CogACT evaluated (few open diffusion-based VLAs). (reviewer inference) No LIBERO or real-robot evaluation in parts read; generality to flow-matching experts (pi0/SmolVLA).

title: A Survey on Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
venue: arXiv (v3, 2026-09-28; no venue in comments field)
efficiency_lever: Taxonomy of three pillars: (1) Efficient Model Design (efficient architectures and model compression); (2) Efficient Training (reducing computational burden during learning); (3) Efficient Data Collection (bottlenecks in acquiring and utilizing robot data)
assumptions: Claims to be the first comprehensive review of efficient VLAs across the model–training–data pipeline (authors' claim).
open_questions: Authors summarize applications, key challenges and future directions (specific items not extracted — only the abstract page was read). Project page: https://evla-survey.github.io/

title: Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion
venue: RSS 2023 (conference version); arXiv PDF read is the extended version (journal not named on the page)
params_and_backbone: Not a VLA (no language model). ResNet-18 vision encoder (~22M, trained end-to-end); CNN-based diffusion net ~22M (45M Transport) or time-series diffusion transformer ~9M (sim) / 80M (Kitchen, real Push-T)
action_generation: diffusion (DDPM, epsilon/noise-prediction MSE objective conditioned on observations); sim: 100 denoising iterations for training and inference; real: DDIM with 100 training / 10 inference iterations (Appendix A.4 says 16 — inconsistent); To=2, Tp=16, Ta=8 (receding-horizon control)
efficiency_lever: Not an efficiency paper; DDIM reduces inference iterations (100 -> 10) and action-sequence prediction with receding horizon amortizes inference over Ta=8 executed actions
reported_gain: '0.1s inference latency on a Nvidia 3080 GPU' (DDIM, 10 inference iterations, real world)
benchmark_success: Average improvement of 46.9% over prior methods (abstract of version read: 15 tasks from 4 benchmarks; Table 3: 12 tasks, 8 sim + 4 real). Third-party: LIBERO avg 72.4 (scratch) in OpenVLA-OFT/SmolVLA tables; Meta-World avg 10.5 in TinyVLA/SmolVLA tables.
assumptions: Sufficient task-specific demonstrations (behavior cloning); actions executed open-loop for Ta steps between replans; multimodal action distributions benefit from diffusion.
tradeoffs: Authors: higher compute and inference latency than simpler methods such as LSTM-GMM; action-sequence prediction may not suffice for high-rate control tasks.
open_questions: Authors: inherits behavior-cloning limits (poor with inadequate demos). (reviewer inference) Few-step / consistency distillation for faster sampling; scaling with language conditioning (addressed by later VLAs).

title: CogACT: A Foundational Vision-Language-Action Model for Synergizing Cognition and Action in Robotic Manipulation
params_and_backbone: 7.6B total (abstract: 7B): DINOv2+SigLIP -> 256 visual tokens, LLaMA-2 language backbone, learnable cognition token; DiT action module Small 13M / Base 89M (default) / Large 308M
action_generation: diffusion: DiT action module conditioned on the VLM cognition feature (cognition feature + noisy action tokens as transformer inputs; denoising step added to cognition feature via sinusoidal encoding); noise-prediction MSE; DDIM 10 inference steps, CFG scale 1.5; predicts current + 15 future actions (16); Adaptive Action Ensemble (α=0.1, C=0.2)
efficiency_lever: Not an efficiency paper; decouples cognition (single feature from 7B VLM) from action generation in a small DiT so multi-step denoising does not re-run the VLM
reported_gain: Inference latency not reported in the paper (A6000/A100 used for sim). Third-party: VLA-Cache measures CogACT 54.29 ms on RTX 4090 (SIMPLER VM); EfficientVLA measures 0.2342 s/step on A40.
benchmark_success: SIMPLER: Google VM 74.8 / VA 61.3 / WidowX VM 51.3 (OpenVLA 34.3/39.3/4.2; RT-2-X 46.3/54.4/–; Octo-Base 11.0/1.2/17.5). Abstract: >35% over OpenVLA in sim, +18% abs over RT-2-X (55B), >55% over OpenVLA on real robots. Realman seen 71.2% vs 12.1%; Franka 61.4% vs 6.8%.
assumptions: A single cognition feature carries sufficient task information for action generation; training on single-arm end-effector OXE subsets with third-person camera.
tradeoffs: 7.6B total still large; 10 DDIM steps + CFG (1.5) per inference; action ensemble adds temporal smoothing at cost of reactivity (reviewer inference).
open_questions: (reviewer inference) Latency not reported; weaker on unseen categories (25.0% on Realman unseen-category task); small evaluation sample (e.g., 11 Franka trials/task); no dedicated limitations section.

title: Leave No Observation Behind: Real-time Correction for VLA Action Chunks
venue: arXiv (v1, 27 Sep 2025; no venue in comments field)
params_and_backbone: Base: SmolVLA (450M, trained from scratch on LIBERO because pretrained embodiment differs) for LIBERO; flow policy for Kinetix. Correction head: ~32M for LIBERO (6-layer transformer encoder + 3-layer MLP), ~0.31M for Kinetix (3-layer MLP, 512 hidden)
action_generation: other: base VLA action chunk (SmolVLA flow matching) + per-step residual correction from a lightweight head conditioned on latest observation, base action, sinusoidal in-chunk index feature, base-policy latent
efficiency_lever: Restore closed-loop reactivity of chunked/asynchronous execution without re-running the large VLA: small correction head runs every control step; orthogonal to RTC
reported_gain: NVIDIA RTX 5080 laptop GPU (16 GB), mean of 100 trials: SmolVLA ~101 ms per inference vs A2C2 head ~4.7 ms per step. Abstract: '+23% point' (Kinetix, 12 tasks) and '+7% point' (LIBERO Spatial) vs RTC.
benchmark_success: LIBERO-Spatial, SmolVLA naive async -> +A2C2 (Table 7; e=exec horizon, d=delay): e40/d10 67->84; e40/d5 66->86; e40/d3 65->86; e40/d1 74->83; e10/d10 75->88; e10/d5 82->92; e10/d3 81->89; e10/d1 83->92; e50/d0 71->84; e40/d0 79->89; e30/d0 79->89; e10/d0 85->87; e5/d0 83->85; e1/d0 77->84. Table 1 gives different values for same settings (e10/d0 81.8->89.2; e40/d10 64.4->84.2; e50/d0 72.2->81.6). Kinetix: >85% at d=4 even at horizon 7.
assumptions: Correction head trained post hoc on the same demonstrations using cached base-policy outputs; no retraining of base VLA; access to base-policy latent features.
tradeoffs: Requires training a (small) extra head per task/embodiment — not training-free; adds ~4.7 ms per control step; LIBERO base SmolVLA trained from scratch (not the pretrained checkpoint); head training sensitive to LR (1e-4 did not work well).
open_questions: Authors: scalability to richer language, OOD settings and more dynamic tasks beyond LIBERO-Spatial needs validation. (reviewer inference) LIBERO tables report no RTC column although abstract claims +7 pts vs RTC on LIBERO Spatial; Table 1 vs Table 7 inconsistent; note SmolVLA naive SR is non-monotonic in e (best e=10, d=0: 85%), consistent with SmolVLA's own chunk-size ablation favoring 10.

title: Real-Time Execution of Action Chunking Flow Policies
params_and_backbone: Applied to pi0.5 (real world) and flow policies on Kinetix (sim); no new model
action_generation: flow matching (base policy) with inference-time guided inpainting; n=5 denoising steps (sim and real); real: H=50, execution horizon s=25, 20 ms control period; sim: H=8, delays 0–4 steps
efficiency_lever: Asynchronous execution without discontinuities: generate next chunk while current executes, freeze actions guaranteed to execute during inference delay, inpaint remaining actions via guidance with exponentially decaying soft mask; guidance weight clipped at β=5
reported_gain: Abstract: remains effective with inference delays >300 ms (>30% of prediction horizon). Real world (6 bimanual tasks, 480 episodes, injected +0/+100/+200 ms ≈ d 6/11/16): best average throughput at every delay, no degradation with delay (sync degrades ~linearly); same motion reported ~20% faster than synchronous (as extracted). Latency on RTX 4090 bf16: RTC 97 ms vs vanilla pi0.5 76 ms (per-denoising-step 14 -> 35 ms due to backprop through each step); BID (N=16) 223 ms.
benchmark_success: Kinetix (12 dynamic tasks): RTC > BID, naive async, temporal ensembling across delays (exact numbers in figures; not extracted). Real-world throughput gains significant at +100 and +200 ms.
assumptions: Base policy is diffusion/flow-based; inference delay d is known/estimated and smaller than the execution horizon; frozen prefix actions will actually be executed.
tradeoffs: Training-free but adds ~21 ms (76 -> 97 ms) per chunk from vector-Jacobian guidance; only for diffusion/flow policies; temporal ensembling fails (averages of valid actions not valid).
open_questions: Authors: significant compute overhead; diffusion/flow only; not tested in more dynamic settings (e.g., legged locomotion). (reviewer inference) Interaction with step-reduction/distillation; A2C2 reports being orthogonal/complementary.

title: Running VLAs at Real-time Speed
params_and_backbone: pi0-level VLA: PaliGemma backbone (SigLIP ~400M + Gemma 2.6B, ~3B) + ~300M action expert.
action_generation: flow matching, 10 action-expert denoising steps (pi0 recipe).
efficiency_lever: Inference-only systems optimisation: CUDA graphs to remove CPU launch overhead (~2x), folding RMSNorm affine and the action-time embedding into adjacent linear layers, fused QKV/RoPE, fused gated linear layers and scalar ops, Triton GEMM tile tuning, dropping the last LLM layer (17 of 18); plus a streaming inference framework.
reported_gain: RTX 4090, bf16, 10 steps (Table 1): 2 views 106.5 ms (naive torch) / 53.7 ms (openpi JAX) -> 27.3 ms; 1 view 20.0 ms; 3 views 36.8 ms; 30 Hz frame rate.
benchmark_success: Real-world falling-pen catching: 10/10 consecutive successes (policy trained with openpi on 600 episodes). No standard benchmark reported.
assumptions: Model weights fixed; a single consumer GPU with native bf16; per-shape kernel tuning for one model and input size.
tradeoffs: Large engineering effort (hand-written/fused kernels) tied to one architecture and GPU; dropping a layer changes the model; no closed-loop success comparison against the unoptimised policy.
open_questions: (reviewer inference) Whether each fused/approximated step leaves closed-loop success unchanged on a standard benchmark; portability to GPUs without bf16 tensor cores.
training_free: yes (speed-ups); the task policy itself was trained

title: When Faster VLA Deployment Changes Closed-Loop Behavior: Task Success-Latency Analysis of SmolVLA Across PyTorch and ONNX Variants
params_and_backbone: Same checkpoint as this study: HuggingFaceVLA/smolvla_libero, LeRobot 0.6.1 (MuJoCo 3.3.2).
efficiency_lever: Runtime change: PyTorch+AMP vs ONNX Runtime (CUDA EP) with 'requested' FP16/INT8 exports; static language width 16/24/32 tokens.
reported_gain: RTX 2060 6 GB, batch 1: PyTorch+AMP p50 903 ms / p99 1181 ms; ONNX p50 537.5-549.2 ms (p99 532-601 ms) - about 2x lower latency.
benchmark_success: LIBERO Spatial / Object, 100 episodes each: PyTorch+AMP 70.0 / 88.0; ONNX width 16 41.0 / 89.0; width 24 75.0 / 90.0; width 32 71.0 / 87.0. Paired 300 episodes, Spatial: 56.7 vs 33.0 (McNemar p = 2.2e-9).
assumptions: One GPU, one checkpoint, one seed; the exported graph has a static language width (width 16 truncates 5 of 10 Spatial instructions).
tradeoffs: Faster runtime but a silent behaviour change: truncated instructions cut Spatial success by ~29 pp; the 'INT8' artifact is a byte-identical FP32 graph, i.e. not real INT8.
open_questions: Authors: factors other than width (graph conversion, AMP vs FP32, kernels, true INT8, TensorRT) not isolated; no equivalence test ('a non-significant two-proportion test is not an equivalence result').

title: Fewer Steps, Better Actions: Rethinking Flow-Matching Inference for VLA Policies
params_and_backbone: Frozen pi0.5 (fine-tuned) and frozen official SmolVLA; corrector parameter count UNVERIFIED (not reported).
action_generation: flow matching with few Euler steps + a learned endpoint correction (lightweight Transformer reading the candidate action, the source noise and the shared prefix cache).
efficiency_lever: Spend part of the integration budget on a learned residual corrector instead of more flow steps.
reported_gain: pi0.5-FT on A100: 10 steps 233.0 ms -> Coda 2 steps 109.9 ms (2.12x); SmolVLA: 233.5 -> 118.1 ms (1.98x).
assumptions: Demonstrations available to train the corrector (SmolVLA: 18,716 steps, batch 256); base policy frozen.
tradeoffs: Requires training and a second network; naive step reduction alone is nearly free for pi0.5 down to 3 steps but collapses at 1 step (and for SmolVLA at 1 step).
open_questions: (reviewer inference) Results are on RoboTwin; whether the same step curve holds on LIBERO and for per-step re-planning.

title: vla.cpp: A Unified Inference Runtime for Vision-Language-Action Models
params_and_backbone: C++ runtime for eleven VLA models (list UNVERIFIED from the abstract); SmolVLA and BitVLA discussed.
action_generation: Architecture-specific heads; iterative policies reuse observation-dependent computation across solver steps.
efficiency_lever: Runtime without PyTorch: shared loading/execution/serving; ternary tensor-core kernel for BitVLA.
reported_gain: BitVLA client inference 4.0-4.6x faster than a CUDA-core baseline on RTX 3060 and AGX Orin.
benchmark_success: LIBERO-Object: BitVLA 200/200 episodes on an 8 GB Jetson Orin Nano; a SmolVLA case study links positional-index precision to gripper commands and task success.
assumptions: Re-implementation of each model in C++ matches the reference behaviour.
tradeoffs: Engineering cost per architecture; numerical details (e.g. positional-index precision) can change closed-loop behaviour.
open_questions: (reviewer inference) Absolute latencies and SmolVLA success rates not given in the abstract.
